hops.afterHeading: Two eyes, one relay: which inputs lose?
hops.title: When synapse density peaks in the human frontal cortex
hops.text: You might expect a growing brain simply to add synapses as it matures. In layer 3 of the human middle frontal gyrus, synapse density rises and falls. In 1979 the pediatric neurologist Peter Huttenlocher counted synaptic profiles per unit volume there in 21 human brains, from newborns to a 90-year-old. Newborn density was already in the adult range. At one to two years it peaked about 50 percent above the adult mean of roughly 1.1 billion synapses per cubic millimeter, then fell between ages two and 16. That rise and fall fits overproduction followed by pruning, like the young mouse visual thalamus, though the human counts leave the mechanism open.

sources.citation: Huttenlocher PR, Synaptic density in human frontal cortex - developmental changes and effects of aging, Brain Research 163(2):195-205 (1979).

image.caption: In one layer of human frontal cortex, synapse density peaks near 1.5 times the adult level by age two.

hops.afterHeading: A tag from the immune system
hops.title: How heating blood serum revealed complement
hops.text: In the 1890s at the Pasteur Institute, Jules Bordet found that the bacteria-killing power of blood serum vanished after 30 minutes at 56 degrees Celsius, although the antibodies in it were heat-stable. In his experiments, killing the bacteria depended on the antibodies and a heat-sensitive factor in the serum working together. Bordet used the older name alexin, from a Greek word meaning to defend. In 1899 Paul Ehrlich, in Berlin, gave it the name that stuck, complement, because it completes the work of antibodies. In 2007 Stevens and colleagues found complement proteins at developing synapses in the young mouse brain, an unexpected place for a system known for immune defense.

sources.citation: Papavergi MT et al., The complement cascade in Alzheimer's disease: modern implications of an ancient immune protagonist, Molecular Neurodegeneration 21:5 (2025); Bardhan M and Kaushik R, Physiology, Complement Cascade, StatPearls (2023).
Bardhan M and Kaushik R, Physiology, Complement Cascade, StatPearls (2023).
Stevens B et al., The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination, Cell 131(6):1164-1178 (2007).

hops.afterHeading: When pruning goes wrong: links, not causes
hops.title: How West Nile infection costs mice their synaptic terminals
hops.text: Some neuroinvasive West Nile survivors have lasting memory and cognitive problems. In 2016 Michael Vasek, Robyn Klein and colleagues tested an attenuated strain most mice survive. As a group, recovered mice learned a maze more slowly than controls, without detectable hippocampal neuron loss. In hippocampal CA3, C1q overlapped more with a presynaptic marker, and microglia held more presynaptic material during acute infection and early recovery. People who died during acute infection had less CA3 presynaptic marker staining than matched controls. Acutely infected mice lacking C3, or with fewer microglia, kept measured CA3 presynaptic terminals. Separately, recovered mice with fewer terminals showed poorer spatial learning, suggesting terminal loss may impair memory.

sources.citation: Vasek MJ et al., A complement-microglial axis drives synapse loss during virus-induced memory impairment, Nature 534(7608):538-543 (2016).
Klee AL et al., Long-term prognosis for clinical West Nile virus infection, Emerging Infectious Diseases 10(8):1405-1411 (2004).
